title: Hunting Gravitational Waves Without a LIGO-Style Detector
hook: LIGO can't see gravitational waves above a few kHz. Physicists just used precision laser spectroscopy instead, setting the first-ever limits across a huge, previously unexplored frequency range.
key_points: Gravitational waves passing through a laser cavity subtly modulate the frequency of the light it emits — a different detection channel than the mirror-displacement method LIGO uses.
Using precision optical spectroscopy, researchers searched for gravitational waves between 100 kHz and 100 MHz, a range essentially unexplored by existing detectors.
They set the first constraints across much of this frequency window.
The team expects future refinements of the technique to improve sensitivity by eight orders of magnitude and extend coverage up to at least 1 GHz.
content_html: Gravitational-wave astronomy has a blind spot: LIGO-style detectors, which sense gravitational waves by measuring tiny displacements of mirrors, lose sensitivity above a few kilohertz. Above that, from the kHz range up through MHz and beyond, we've had essentially no way to look.
extra_html: Physicists Dmitry Budker, Valerie Domcke, Joachim Kopp, and Oleg Tretiak use a different physical effect entirely: a gravitational wave passing through a laser cavity subtly modulates the frequency of the light it emits. By applying precision optical spectroscopy to search for that modulation, the team set the first constraints on gravitational waves across much of the 100 kHz to 100 MHz range — a huge swath of the spectrum previously unexplored by any detector. The current limits aren't yet competitive with the most optimistic theoretical predictions, but the team expects future refinements to push sensitivity up by eight orders of magnitude and extend coverage to at least 1 GHz, opening a genuinely new observational window that could catch exotic high-frequency sources invisible to LIGO.

related.title: Gravitational Waves: Ripples in Spacetime
related.hook: When black holes collide, they shake the fabric of spacetime itself, sending out ripples that stretch and squeeze everything they pass — by less than the width of a proton.

related.title: 390 Gravitational Waves In, and Black Hole Astronomy Is Just Getting Started
related.hook: The latest gravitational-wave catalog leaps to 390 confirmed detections — including the clearest signal ever caught and evidence some black holes are built from earlier mergers.

flashcards.prompt: How does this technique detect gravitational waves, and how is that different from LIGO?
flashcards.back_html: A passing gravitational wave subtly modulates the frequency of light emitted by a laser cavity — detected via precision spectroscopy, rather than LIGO's approach of measuring tiny mirror displacements with laser interferometry.
